meta.ogDescription: Art News, November 1963 — but the tape of the Swenson interview does not carry the first-person sentence at all.

answer.label: As printed, credited to
answer.sourceLine: Art News printed this sentence under Warhol’s name in November 1963, in G. R. Swenson’s ‘What is Pop Art? Answers from 8 Painters’, Part 1 — the text Wikiquote carries ↗. But the surviving cassette of that interview, transcribed by Jennifer Sichel in the Oxford Art Journal in 2018 ↗, does not carry the first-person sentence: what Warhol says on the tape is “everybody should be a machine”, inside an exchange about homosexuality that Art News editor Thomas Hess cut. Warhol was in the room — this wording is the magazine’s.

source.excerpt: The reason I’m painting this way is that I want to be a machine, and I feel that whatever I do and do machine-like is what I want to do.
trail: Wikiquote lists the sentence verbatim among the sourced 1960s quotations on its Andy Warhol page ↗, with a full citation — interviewer, article, magazine, volume and month: ‘What is Pop Art? Answers from 8 Painters’, Part 1, G. R. Swenson, in Art News 62 (November 1963). That establishes what the magazine printed, not what was said in the room.
Wikipedia’s article on Warhol’s 1963–64 Self-Portraits ↗ quotes the full sentence and footnotes it to the scanned November 1963 issue of ARTnews.
That issue exists as a digitised object: the Internet Archive holds Art News 1963-11: Vol 62 Iss 7 ↗. It is an access-restricted item, so we could confirm the issue but not read the page ourselves.

In 2018 Jennifer Sichel published the surviving cassette of the interview: ‘What is Pop Art?’ A Revised Transcript of Gene Swenson’s 1963 Interview with Andy Warhol ↗, Oxford Art Journal 41.1, pp. 85–100, alongside her essay ‘Do you think Pop Art’s queer?’ Gene Swenson and Andy Warhol ↗ (pp. 59–83). The recording shows the published interview was heavily edited and reconfigured — Swenson opened by asking Warhol about homosexuality, a topic absent from the printed version entirely.

Gary Comenas, whose 1963 chronology this page also cites, puts the consequence plainly on Warholstars ↗: “Warhol never said he wanted to be a machine.” The tapes have him saying “everybody should be a machine” — during a conversation about men, women and homosexuality, the point being that people should be as judgmental as a machine, which is to say not judgmental at all.

The line was already circulating in print — in its clipped form — by 1971, when Robert Hughes wrote in Time ↗: “Says Andy with utter sincerity: ‘I want to be a machine’ — which to him means never to make choices.”
source.excerptNote: The excerpt above is the sentence as Art News printed it, not a transcript of the tape. Wikiquote lists a second exchange from the same interview separately: “Andy Warhol: I think everybody should like everybody. / Gene Swenson: Is that what Pop Art is all about? / Andy Warhol: Yes, it’s liking things.” The tape research puts the two closer together than the printed article does — on the recording, the machine remark belongs to the same passage about liking everybody and not judging people.

author.name: Andy Warhol
author.heading: Who was Andy Warhol?
author.bio: Born in Pittsburgh in 1928, Warhol worked as a commercial illustrator in New York before turning the vocabulary of advertising on fine art — silkscreened soup cans, Coke bottles, Marilyns and car crashes, made in series and largely by other people’s hands. By 1964 he was working out of the foil-lined studio at 231 East 47th Street known as the Factory, a name that doubled as a thesis. He went on to make experimental films, found Interview magazine and manage the Velvet Underground, survived being shot in 1968, and died in 1987.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The byline is right — Warhol sat for this interview — but very little downstream of it is. What circulates is the clipped half of a sentence that the magazine had already reworked, and the recording that survives says something else.

items.who: Andy Warhol — but only half of him
items.why: Almost every repost stops at “I want to be a machine.” The sentence Art News printed keeps going: “…and I feel that whatever I do and do machine-like is what I want to do.” The short form is not a modern invention — Robert Hughes was already using it in Time in May 1971 ↗, where it appears bare as “I want to be a machine.”

items.who: The printed wording — not what the tape carries
items.why: In 2018 Jennifer Sichel published the surviving cassette of the interview in the Oxford Art Journal (41.1 — transcript pp. 85–100, essay pp. 59–83), and it does not carry the first-person sentence. What Warhol says is “everybody should be a machine”, in an exchange about men, women and homosexuality and about not judging people — a conversation the published article removed. Warhol’s biographer David Bourdon had already called the interview “troublesome for art historians”: Swenson concealed his tape recorder, and some of the more “intellectual”-sounding answers “may have been doctored by Swenson”. The specialist site this page cites for that caveat, Warholstars ↗, now states the conclusion outright: “Warhol never said he wanted to be a machine.”

The line is usually reposted with no source at all, or with a bare “1963” and nothing else — even though the full citation has sat in the open for years in the sourced section of Wikiquote’s Andy Warhol page ↗, complete with interviewer, magazine, volume and month. That citation tells you what Art News printed; for what was said you need Sichel’s transcript of the tape.

misattribution.truthLine: What is established: Art News printed this sentence under Warhol’s name in November 1963, in Swenson’s ‘What is Pop Art? Answers from 8 Painters’, Part 1. What the surviving tape carries is “everybody should be a machine” — so the famous first-person line is the magazine’s wording, not a documented Warhol sentence.

context.heading: Why everyone quotes a sentence Warhol didn’t say
lead: By late 1963 Warhol had already given up the brushwork that was supposed to certify an artist’s soul. He was making silkscreen paintings of supermarket goods and dead celebrities — images pushed through a mesh rather than drawn by hand — and the obvious hostile question, where are you in this?, was waiting for an answer. Art News supplied one in November 1963, in the sentence everybody still quotes. It fitted the work so exactly, and the studio that followed, that for fifty-five years nobody checked it: Warhol moved into 231 East 47th Street, the foil-lined space known as the Factory, and the work came out in series, made largely by assistants, with the artist’s hand deliberately minimised.

When somebody finally did check, the tape said something else. On the recording Warhol is talking about men, women and homosexuality, and about liking everybody; the line is that everybody should be a machine — a machine as a model of not judging people, not a painter’s manifesto. That conversation never reached print. The printed version did, and it became a thesis: the National Galleries of Scotland built its 2018–19 Warhol/Paolozzi show on the quotation, which is the moment Gary Comenas pointed out it was never said. Robert Hughes had glossed the phrase in Time in 1971 as meaning “never to make choices” — a reading of a sentence, it turns out, that an editor helped write.
context.detailsSummary: A note on how much of this interview is really Warhol
detailsBody: The 1963 Swenson interview is the source of several of Warhol’s best-known lines, and the reason to doubt it is not new. Warhol was reportedly unwilling that day, Swenson concealed his tape recorder, and the biographer David Bourdon suspected the more articulate passages had been tidied in the writing — his named example being a remark about the literary quarterly the Hudson Review, which Warhol was not known to read. “Particularly” is the word Bourdon uses about that example: he offers it as the clearest case, not as the boundary of his suspicion.

Sichel’s transcript is what turned the suspicion into a finding, and it reaches this sentence. William S. Wilson, who knew both men, described the mechanism: Swenson’s interviews “were not printed as he submitted them to Art News, because Thomas Hess changed words in both questions and responses, editing Art News as a magazine for a wholesome family.” So the machine line stays on this page as what the magazine published under Warhol’s name — not as something anyone can show he said.
context.pull: Warhol never said he wanted to be a machine.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists, in its sourced 1960s section for Andy Warhol, the exact wording "The reason I'm painting this way is that I want to be a machine, and I feel that whatever I do and do machine-like is what I want to do." cited to 'What is Pop Art? Answers from 8 Painters', Part 1, G. R. Swenson, in Art News 62 (November 1963); it also has a subsection for that interview noting the 1969 reprint in Pop Art Redefined, eds. John Russell and Suzi Gablik, and records the separate exchange "I think everybody should like everybody. / Is that what Pop Art is all about? / Yes, it's liking things."

The English Wikipedia article on Warhol's 1963-64 Self-Portraits quotes the full sentence and cites it to Swenson, G. R., 'What Is Pop Art?', ARTnews, vol. 62, iss. 7, November 1963, linking the Internet Archive scan of that issue.
The Internet Archive item sim_artnews_1963-11_62_7 is the digitised 'Art News 1963-11: Vol 62 Iss 7' and is an access-restricted (non-borrowable) item.

Robert Hughes's Time article 'Art: Man for the Machine' (17 May 1971) contains: Says Andy with utter sincerity: "I want to be a machine" - which to him means never to make choices; the article gives no source for the quotation.

The Warholstars 1963 chronology quotes Warhol biographer David Bourdon: "This widely quoted interview is troublesome for art historians. Swenson and Warhol were good friends, but the artist was in one of his uncooperative moods, prompting the critic to conceal his tape recorder during the interview. Some of the more 'intellectual' sounding quotes attributed to Warhol may have been doctored by Swenson, particularly the remarks concerning the Hudson Review, a literary quarterly that Warhol was not known to read."

Wikipedia's Andy Warhol article gives his birth as 6 August 1928 in Pittsburgh and death as 22 February 1987, describes his silkscreen paintings of consumer products and celebrities, the Factory at 231 East 47th Street from 1964, the founding of Interview magazine, his management of the Velvet Underground and the 1968 assassination attempt; it does not mention the Swenson interview or the machine quotation.

Gary Comenas's Warholstars page 'Did Andy Warhol want to be a machine?' states: "But, as recent research by Jennifer Sichel showed (published in the Oxford Art Journal), Warhol never said he wanted to be a machine." It reports that "the original interview tapes show that Warhol did say that 'everybody should be a machine' but it was during a conversation about men and woman and homosexuality and how everyone should like 'everything,' including homosexuality. The point that was being made was that people should be as judgmental as a machine, which was to say, not judgemental at all." It quotes William S. Wilson that Swenson's "interviews with artists were not printed as he submitted them to Art News, because Thomas Hess changed words in both questions and responses, editing Art News as a magazine for a wholesome family", cites Jennifer Sichel, 'Do you think Pop Art's queer? Gene Swenson and Andy Warhol', Oxford Art Journal, Vol. 41, issue 1, March 2018, pp. 59-83, and dates the National Galleries of Scotland Warhol/Paolozzi show to 17 November 2018 - 2 June 2019.

Oxford Academic's record for Jennifer Sichel, "'What is Pop Art?' A Revised Transcript of Gene Swenson's 1963 Interview with Andy Warhol", Oxford Art Journal vol. 41, iss. 1, pp. 85-100, published 21 February 2018, describes cassette recordings found in Swenson's archive showing the source material was heavily edited and reconfigured for publication in ARTnews, with controversial and explicitly queer content excised; Swenson opened the conversation with a direct question about homosexuality, absent from the published interview.

Oxford Academic's record for Jennifer Sichel, "'Do you think Pop Art's queer?' Gene Swenson and Andy Warhol", Oxford Art Journal vol. 41, iss. 1, pp. 59-83, March 2018 (online 21 February 2018), doi 10.1093/oxartj/kcx044, describes the recovered recording of the 1963 ARTnews interview and the removal of the discussion of homosexuality from the published version.

The Warholstars page on Warhol's 1963-64 self-portraits states, of Sichel's examination of the original Swenson tapes, "He never actually said that he wanted to paint like a machine", and that Warhol "did not say much of what he was quoted as saying".

Quote Investigator has no article on Warhol's 'want to be a machine' line - a site search for 'Warhol' returns only articles on 'only genius with an IQ of 85', 'famous for being famous', 'openings of envelopes' and the two '15 minutes' pieces.
